A Skeptic's Guide to Cryptocurrency and Stablecoins

Eisman asks fintech strategist Rahul Jindal to explain why crypto should hedge monetary stress, how stablecoins work, and what they add to existing payment networks. He separates payment infrastructure from token speculation and presses the guest on switching costs, trust and Visa’s services. The dialogue also exposes confusion about Bitcoin divisibility, SOL versus stablecoins, and Visa+ reach. Jindal closes with crypto legislation and a preference for industry-specific payments software.

YouTube · 2025-06-02 ↗Substack · 2025-06-08 ↗
Eisman’s strongest contribution is the demand for a concrete use case, an observable thesis and an identified economic beneficiary. That framework is more defensible than several technical premises: the finite Bitcoin supply does not prevent fractional payments, Visa+ was not universal global app interoperability, and his 2023 market-loss chronology is wrong. Jindal’s near-term stablecoin-law prediction succeeded, while his year-end 2025 market-structure-law expectation missed. The guest’s momentary treatment of SOL as a dollar-backed stablecoin is explicitly separated from Eisman’s correction.

  • Tether reserve-representation enforcement order · 2021-10-15
    The order found misleading historical reserve representations and sufficient fiat reserves on only 27.6% of days in its 2016-18 sample. Historical misconduct does not establish current insolvency.
  • GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27 · 2025-07-18
    Enacted July 18. The law permits qualifying state oversight at no more than $10 billion of outstanding issuance, with transition rules and waivers above the threshold. Federal regulator responsibilities depend on issuer type.

How he reasons here

  • Separate a token investment, a stablecoin claim and the payment network that carries it.
  • Ask what behavior the thesis predicts, while distinguishing a single trading day from a long-horizon hedge test.
  • Compare total payment costs, fraud protection, settlement, refunds and switching costs.
  • Check who earns reserve yield and who captures network economics.
  • Prefer understandable businesses and test whether a new technology complements incumbents.
  • Reserve quality and redemption rights matter more than the label stable.

Tools and charts discussed

Mentioned in the transcript; visual charts have not all been inspected.

  • Crypto/equity return correlation across regimes, with window and frequency specified.
  • Reserve-backed token issuance, custody, redemption and reserve yield.
  • Network fees versus issuer interchange and total merchant discount.
  • Visa+, Visa Direct, stablecoin rails and cross-border remittance use cases.
  • Legislative milestones and state/federal issuer-supervision thresholds.
  • Industry-specific software, merchant retention and payment processing.
